chapter_en: The Decrees on Food of Non-Jews

sections.title_en: The Attitude Towards Non-Jews and the Decrees to Prevent Assimilation
sections.body_en:
As a fence against assimilation, the Sages decreed that Jews should not eat the bread of non-Jews, the cooked food of non-Jews or the wine of non-Jews. Admittedly, there is a mitzva to love every person without distinction of race or religion, as our forefather Avraham did, who opened his tent to all passers-by. And this is the destiny of the people of Israel, to bring blessing to all the nations, as it was said to our forefather Avraham (Bereshit 12:2-3): "And I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, and you shall be a blessing… and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed." And likewise it was said to our forefather Yitzḥak (ibid. 26:4): "And in your seed all the nations of the earth shall bless themselves." And likewise it was said to our forefather Ya'akov (ibid. 28:14): "And in you and in your seed all the families of the earth shall be blessed." And as our master Rav Kook wrote, love of all creatures "must extend to all of humanity, despite all the differences of opinions, religions and beliefs, and despite all the distinctions of races and climates." "Love of all creatures must be alive in the heart and the soul – love of every person individually, and love of all the nations together… for a point of life, light and holiness never departs from the divine image with which humanity as a whole was graced, and with which every nation and tongue was graced, each according to its value." And hatred must be directed only towards the wickedness that binds the nations together and sweeps the wicked into deeds of wickedness and corruption (Middot Ha-Re'aya, Ahava, sections 5; 10).

However, in order for the people of Israel to be able to bring blessing to all human beings, it must cleave to the Torah and the mitzvot, establish a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, and reveal the sacred value in every field and thing in the world, so that the divine light and its blessing will spread to all the realms of Israel's life, and from this, inspiration and blessing will spread to all the nations. For this purpose the people of Israel must preserve its uniqueness and set up a fence that will prevent its children from assimilating among the nations and forgetting their destiny. And since foods bring hearts closer together, the Sages established decrees intended to distinguish Israel from the non-Jews, that Jews should not eat the foods of non-Jews, such as wine, bread and cooked foods, even when they are made from kosher products.

Regarding a similar matter, our teacher and rabbi, Rav Tzvi Yehuda Kook, would repeatedly emphasise: "Distinction is not separation," and he added that when this statement becomes widely known, redemption will come to the world. For this understanding makes it possible to reveal the uniqueness of every person and nation in a moral manner, without harming the dignity of other nations and the good relations that should exist among all human beings.

Sometimes, however, it is not possible to suffice with a respectful distinction between Israel and the nations, because when nations and groups are drawn after evil and choose wickedness, it is necessary to denounce them and to distance and separate oneself from them and from their wickedness. And in order to fence Israel off from their influence, the Sages enacted a severe decree on wine that an idol worshipper touched, that it be forbidden even for benefit. Thus all the distancings from the foods of non-Jews were intended for these two purposes: to create the distinct space unique to Israel, and to distance Israel from cultures in which wickedness is prominent.

This principle is explained in the Torah with regard to all the food prohibitions, which were intended to distinguish Israel and sanctify them, as it is stated (Vayikra 20:24-26): "… I am the Lord your God, who has set you apart from the peoples. You shall therefore distinguish between the pure animal and the impure, and between the impure bird and the pure, and you shall not make your souls abominable by animal or by bird or by anything that creeps on the ground, which I have set apart for you as impure. And you shall be holy to Me, for I the Lord am holy, and I have set you apart from the peoples to be Mine." And likewise we learned that Jews' eating of the foods of non-Jews may lead to assimilation and idolatry, as it is stated (Shemot 34:15-16): "Lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, and they go astray after their gods and sacrifice to their gods, and one invites you and you eat of his sacrifice; and you take of their daughters for your sons, and their daughters go astray after their gods and make your sons go astray after their gods."1

notes_en.en: Admittedly, the prohibition of eating from the sacrifices of the non-Jews (Shemot 34:15) applies in its plain sense to eating from idolatrous sacrifices (so wrote the Ramban, Semag and Ḥinukh in explaining the verse); however, the Sages learned that the prohibition also applies to participating in a feast of idol-worshipping non-Jews, even though the foods there are kosher (Ḥullin 8a; Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 9:15; SA 152:1). Likewise, the Rambam (Hilkhot Sheḥita 4:11-12) learned from this verse that the slaughter of a non-Jew, even when performed according to halakha, is invalid. And the Rashba (Torat Ha-bayit Ha-katzar 3:7) and the Issur Ve-heter He-arokh (43:1) based the prohibition of the bread and cooked food of non-Jews on this verse. It is worth noting that through the decree on the cooked food of non-Jews a fence was also set up against eating forbidden foods, such as nevelot, pork, sheratzim and mixtures of meat and milk, which are commonly found in the kitchens of non-Jews (Rashi, Avoda Zara 38a).

sections.body_en:
Among the decrees that the Sages enacted concerning the foods of non-Jews, the prohibition they decreed on wine is the most severe of them. As the Sages said (Avoda Zara 36b): "They decreed on their bread because of their wine, and on their wine because of their daughters, and on their daughters because of 'something else' (idolatry)." That is, the essence of the decree was that people should not drink their wine, and thereby they set up the most important fence against assimilation and idolatry. And so that people would not come to drink their wine, they also decreed not to eat the bread of non-Jews and the cooked food of non-Jews. And although as a rule one does not enact a decree upon a decree, because of the severity of the concern of assimilation they enacted a decree upon a decree. Furthermore, the Sages were concerned that if they did not decree a prohibition on the bread and cooked food of non-Jews, the prohibition of wine too would be breached; consequently, all the decrees are considered one decree (Ramban, 36b).

Already when Israel was in the wilderness, the need arose to decree a prohibition on the wine of non-Jews. The Sages said (Sanhedrin 106a) that after Bil'am son of Be'or failed to curse Israel, he proposed to Balak king of Moav to cause Israel to sin through harlotry, so that they would anger their God and be punished. For this purpose he proposed setting up, near the camp of Israel, tents for selling white linen garments, which the young men of Israel craved to wear, and to seat in them harlots as saleswomen, an old woman outside and a young woman inside. After the young men of Israel had eaten and drunk and were merry, they went out for a stroll and found before them a market of linen garments, and the old woman would offer the garment at its usual price, and the young woman would peek out of the tent and offer it at half price. He would go in and buy from the young woman. So they did two and three times, until they became acquainted, and the young woman would say to him: You are like a member of the household with me; sit and choose a fine garment for yourself. And skins of wine were placed beside her, and the wine of non-Jews had not yet been forbidden, and she offered him to drink. Once he had drunk, his desire began to burn within him and he sought to sin with her. She took an idol out of her bosom and said to him: "Worship this and I will do as you wish." He said to her: "But I am a Jew!" She said to him: "What do you care? Is anything asked of you but to uncover yourself?" (to relieve oneself before the idol). And he did not know that this is the worship of Ba'al Pe'or, that people relieve themselves before it. And out of his wine and his desire he would uncover himself before the idol and sin with her and deny the Torah of Moshe his teacher. As it is stated (Bamidbar 25:1-9): "And Israel dwelt in Shittim, and the people began to commit harlotry with the daughters of Moav. And they called the people to the sacrifices of their gods, and the people ate and bowed down to their gods. And Israel attached itself to Ba'al Pe'or, and the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel."

And even Zimri son of Salu, one of the heads of the ancestral houses of the tribe of Shimon, breached the fence and sinned with Kozbi daughter of Tzur, of the princes of Midian, before the eyes of Moshe and the people, and many were drawn after him. And the Lord began to strike Israel with a plague, twenty-four thousand men, until Pinḥas son of Elazar the kohen arose and killed Zimri and Kozbi, and the sinners recoiled and the plague was stopped. Rabbi Elazar Ha-moda'i said (Pirkei De-Rabbi Eliezer 46): "Pinḥas arose and placed Israel under a ban, by the secret of the Ineffable Name, and by the writing inscribed on the Tablets, and by the ban of the heavenly court and the ban of the earthly court, that no man of Israel should drink of the wine of non-Jews… for all their wine is for idolatry and harlotry." Apparently, after Israel entered the Land and settled in their place, this prohibition was forgotten.

At the end of the days of the First Temple, after Nevukhadnetzar king of Babylonia conquered the kingdom of Yehuda, as he did in all the kingdoms he conquered, he took captive youths from the noble families of Jerusalem, among them Daniel, Ḥananya, Misha'el and Azarya, in order to raise them in his palace in the ways of Babylonian culture, so that they would identify with his people and his religion, and when they grew up they would help him rule over the members of their own people. Meanwhile, while they were still young, he used holding them in captivity to threaten the nobles of the nations, that if they rebelled against him, he would execute their children. Unlike the youths of the other nations, who within a short time sought to resemble the victorious Babylonians and behave like them, Daniel wished to preserve his identity and cleave to the faith of his fathers, and so that he would not be influenced by Babylonian culture, he took upon himself to abstain from eating their bread, their wine and their oil. As it is stated (Daniel 1:8): "But Daniel resolved in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king's food, nor with the wine of his drinking." "The wine of his drinking" means two drinks: wine and oil. Since he forbade himself to eat their oil, consequently he also refrained from eating their cooked dishes, since people are accustomed to flavour cooked dishes with oil. And so did his companions with him, Ḥananya, Misha'el and Azarya, who sufficed with seeds and legumes. Nevertheless, by the kindness of God, Daniel and his companions looked better and healthier than all the youths who ate of the king's food (Daniel chapter 1; Avoda Zara 36a).

By virtue of their abstention from the foods of non-Jews they succeeded in withstanding the test, and they kept the Torah and the mitzvot in the palace of the king of Babylonia, and served as an example and model of self-sacrifice for preserving Jewish identity in difficult conditions.

Apparently, after Daniel became the great sage of the generation, he guided the people to observe these fences so that they would not assimilate among the non-Jews. However, many of the people of his generation did not follow his ways and enjoyed the feasts of non-Jews, and as the Sages said, the decree of annihilation by Haman and Aḥashverosh was decreed "because they enjoyed the feast of that wicked man" (Megilla 12a). However, "Mordekhai knew all that had been done (Esther 4:1)… he knew for which sin they had been stricken – for having eaten the cooked food of non-Jews" (Yalkut Shimoni, Esther 1056).2

And although in that generation Daniel's guidance had not yet been accepted throughout Israel, by virtue of the faith and courage of Daniel and those who followed his path, Israel merited to be redeemed, to return to the Land and to build the Second Temple. About four hundred years later, the Sages again decreed on the wine of non-Jews and the foods of non-Jews, and their decree was accepted and has endured for all generations.

notes_en.en: In the discussion of oil in the Gemara, Avoda Zara 36a, it is explained that according to Rav, Daniel decreed upon Israel that they should not eat the oil of non-Jews, as it is stated (Daniel 1:8): "But Daniel resolved in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king's food, nor with the wine of his drinking." Thus his decree was on bread, wine and oil, and so wrote the Rid, Ra'avad and Ra'ah (and some hold that he decreed only on oil; see Rashbam in Tosafot, and Ritva). It is not possible that Daniel decreed this while he was a youth; rather, according to Rav, since this is what is stated in the verse (which was written by the Men of the Great Assembly, as explained in Bava Batra 15a), it implies that out of his experience, when he became the great sage of the generation, he together with his companions decreed this upon the whole people. On the other hand, according to Shmuel, "Daniel resolved in his heart" to be careful about this, but he did not instruct all Israel to do so, and only about four hundred years later did the students of Shammai and Hillel decree it. See below in note 4.

sections.title_en: The Development of the Decree on Bread, Wine and Oil
sections.body_en:
In the period before the destruction of the Second Temple, at a tense assembly in the upper chamber of the house of Ḥananya ben Ḥizkiya, the students of Beit Shammai disagreed with the students of Beit Hillel, and when they stood for a vote, Beit Shammai were found to be the majority, and they enacted eighteen decrees on that day. Most of the decrees dealt with adding fences in the laws of impurity and purity, mainly in matters that disqualify the terumot that the kohanim would eat in purity, and they also decreed on the wine, bread and oil of non-Jews (Shabbat 13b; 17b; Avoda Zara 35b).

The dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel was one of principle: Beit Shammai tended to be strict and stringent, and held that in order to fortify the observance of the Torah, additional decrees and fences should be established. Beit Hillel, on the other hand, held that it is preferable to make an effort in education and to be lenient and minimise decrees, for anyone who adds too many decrees detracts, and causes the public to stumble through decrees that it finds difficult to keep. As a rule, the halakha was ruled according to Beit Hillel, who were the majority and whose words were more accepted in the eyes of God and man. As the Sages said (Eruvin 13b): "For three years Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagreed… A heavenly voice went forth and said: These and these are the words of the living God, and the halakha is according to Beit Hillel… because they were gentle and humble, and they would teach their own words and the words of Beit Shammai. And not only that, but they would put the words of Beit Shammai before their own." However, at that assembly Beit Shammai outnumbered Beit Hillel, and when the sages of Beit Hillel sought to disperse the assembly and continue discussing these matters at a later time, the sages of Beit Shammai planted a sword in the study hall and demanded that the halakha be decided, and the halakha was ruled according to Beit Shammai.

Concerning those decrees, Rabbi Eliezer, who leaned towards Beit Shammai, said: "On that day they heaped up the measure," that is, they established fences in a fine and good measure, to fence the people off from transgressions. And Rabbi Yehoshua, who was of Beit Hillel, said: "On that day they levelled it [the measure]," that is, they decreed too many decrees that it is difficult for the public to keep, and as a result of transgressing the decrees of the Sages people are drawn to transgress Torah prohibitions as well (Yerushalmi Shabbat 1:4; Rashi, Shabbat 153b).3

notes_en.en:
Ḥananya ben Ḥizkiya was one of the great sages of the generation, and he and his circle wrote "Megillat Ta'anit," in which were listed the festive days on which it is forbidden to fast, and it was the first document written by the Sages after the sealing of the Tanakh. Of him they said: "But that man is remembered for good, and Ḥananya ben Ḥizkiya is his name, for were it not for him – the book of Yeḥezkel would have been hidden away, because its words contradicted the words of the Torah. What did he do? They brought up to him three hundred jugs of oil, and he sat in the upper chamber and expounded it." From time to time the Sages gathered at his home for halakhic discussions, and although as a rule Beit Hillel were the majority, on one occasion, when discussions of principle arose, "they were counted and Beit Shammai outnumbered Beit Hillel, and they decreed eighteen matters on that day." Thus the decrees were enacted according to the opinion of Beit Shammai. (See Mishna and Gemara Shabbat 13b.)
They said in the Yerushalmi (Shabbat 1:4): "That day was as hard for Israel as the day on which the [golden] calf was made (because of the terrible tension that arose and nearly reached bloodshed)… Rabbi Yehoshua taught… The students of Beit Shammai stood below and were killing (a hyperbolic expression) students of Beit Hillel." That is, the students of Hillel wished to leave and cancel the assembly before the vote, so that a decision according to Beit Shammai would not be accepted on the basis of a chance majority. But the students of Shammai "planted a sword in the study hall," to express the gravity of the matter from their perspective, that no one may leave or enter, and a decision must be made. And the sages of Beit Shammai were the majority, and the decrees were sealed according to their words, and among the decrees they also decreed on the wine, bread and oil of non-Jews (Shabbat 17a-b; Rambam in the Commentary on the Mishna; Ra'avan; Ḥatam Sofer there. And see Yerushalmi Shabbat 1:4, that some hold that bread and oil were decreed by agreement from the outset). Since these decrees were sealed amid great tension and with self-sacrifice, it was agreed that it is forbidden to annul them, and even the sages of Beit Hillel did not challenge them. However, in practice, because of the difficulties the people had in keeping the decrees, after several generations those who continued the path of Beit Hillel eroded them, as explained in the next halakha.

sections.title_en: The Fate of the Decrees and the Permitting of Oil
sections.body_en:
Although as a rule Beit Hillel were the majority, and this majority grew over the generations, the sages of Beit Hillel did not seek to challenge the validity of the decrees, since they were accepted decisively with self-sacrifice. This is what they said (Avoda Zara 36a): "In all matters a court may annul the words of another court, except for the eighteen matters, for even if Eliyahu and his court were to come, we would not listen to him."

However, in practice, following the destruction of the Temple and the cessation of purity in Israel, most of the eighteen decrees became void of their own accord. Not only that, but it became clear that the concern of the sages of Beit Hillel was well founded, and many Jews found it difficult to keep the decree on oil, which was very much needed for food. The more the troubles increased and Israel was dispossessed of its land, the greater the difficulty grew. Until, about two hundred and fifty years after the prohibition was established, at the beginning of the days of the Amora'im, the Sages examined and found that the decree on oil had not spread among the majority of Israel, and Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'a, the grandson of Rabbi [Yehuda Ha-nasi], arose and together with his court annulled the decree prohibiting oil. For in addition to the rule that it is forbidden to annul a decree of the Sages, the Sages stated another rule: "One does not enact a decree upon the public unless the majority of the public can abide by it." And this is what Rabbi Simlai testified: "Oil – Rabbi Yehuda (Nesi'a) and his court were counted concerning it and permitted it."

When the report of the permitting of oil reached Babylonia, the great Amora Rav did not wish to accept it, for while he was still in the Land of Israel he had opposed the initiative to annul the decree on oil, and he held that it stemmed from a lack of respect for those who enacted the decree. However, his colleague Shmuel warned him that if he refused to eat the oil of non-Jews, he would proclaim him a "zaken mamre" (a rebellious elder) who disputes the ruling of the Great Court, and Rav acceded to eat the oil of non-Jews (Yerushalmi Shabbat 1:4). And so it was ruled in the Rambam (Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 17:22): "The oil of non-Jews is permitted, and one who forbids it stands in great sin, because he rebelled against the ruling of the court that permitted it."4

The decree prohibiting the bread of non-Jews was also difficult for Israel to keep, and based on things that Rabbi Yehuda Ha-nasi said, people were accustomed to be lenient in a pressing situation with "pat palter," that is, bread that a non-Jewish baker baked in his bakery for the public (below 28:2). However, the prohibition of wine remained in force and was even strengthened (below 29:1).

notes_en.en:
The decree on oil did not spread among the majority of Israel because of the difficulty of keeping it, for since oil was very much needed, obtaining it sometimes involved mortal danger, as they said in the Yerushalmi (Shabbat 1:4): "They would go up for it to the King's Mountain and be killed over it." However, there were those who kept the decree with devotion, and it is explained in the Bavli (Avoda Zara 36a) that Rav did not wish to accept the annulment of the decree on oil, for how could a decree enacted by Daniel be annulled (as explained in note 1), and he held that Rabbi Simlai did not properly respect the decree and influenced Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'a to permit it (Yerushalmi Avoda Zara 2:4; Shabbat 1:4). And according to Shmuel, the prohibition of oil was not decreed by Daniel; rather, the students of Shammai and Hillel forbade it out of concern that it absorbed a forbidden taste from the pots of non-Jews, and although it is a spoiled taste, they held that "noten ta'am li-fgam" (a taste that spoils) is forbidden. However, Tosafot (s.v. "bi-shlama") explained that even Shmuel agrees that it is proper to abstain from the oil of non-Jews because of ḥatnut (intermarriage, i.e. assimilation), but there was no binding decree about this, only a custom of Daniel. And since the concern of ḥatnut with oil is a remote concern, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel strengthened the decree with the concern of a forbidden taste absorbed in the oil. And since the concern of ḥatnut also stood at the basis of the decree, the decree on oil applied even to oil that was in a pot in which forbidden food had never been cooked. And when it was ruled in practice that noten ta'am li-fgam is permitted, the halakhic basis that was intended to establish the decree became void. (And according to the Ra'avad and Ritva there, according to Shmuel the entire decree on oil is only because of what is emitted from utensils, and not because of ḥatnut.)
The Rishonim disagreed regarding the status of the eighteen decrees. Some say, based on the Yerushalmi, that they have a special status since they were accepted with self-sacrifice, and therefore only a decree that did not spread among the majority of Israel, that is, which the majority of Israel did not practise, may be annulled. But the other decrees that the Sages enacted, even if they spread among the majority of Israel, a court that is greater in wisdom and in number can annul (Tosafot s.v. "ve-hatnan"). And according to many of the Rishonim, the eighteen decrees have no special status; rather, their law is like that of decrees which the public can abide by and which spread throughout Israel, and therefore even a greater court cannot annul them. And a decree that the public can keep but which in practice did not spread in Israel – only a court that is greater in wisdom and in number can annul it, but if it is not greater, it cannot annul it. And if it became clear that it is a decree that the public is unable to keep, even a lesser court can annul it (Ra'avad, Ra'ah, Ritva and Ran). And according to the Rambam (Hilkhot Mamrim 2:2-3), if the decree was established as an enactment of the Sages and spread in Israel, a greater court can annul it. And if it was established as a fence around a Torah prohibition and spread in Israel, like the eighteen decrees, even a greater court cannot annul them. And if it did not spread in Israel, even if it was decreed as a fence around a Torah prohibition, even a lesser court can annul it, as was the case with oil.

sections.title_en: The Decree on the Cooked Food of Non-Jews, and a Summary of the Decrees
sections.body_en:
The Sages enacted a further decree in order to prevent assimilation, that Jews should not eat bishul akum (the cooked food of non-Jews). Thus there are two types of decrees serving as a fence against assimilation: the first on bread, wine and oil, the second on the cooked food of non-Jews.

The first has its root in the custom of Daniel and his companions and its continuation in the decrees of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, that Jews should not eat the bread, wine and oil of non-Jews. These foods are the most important to man, and as stated in the Torah, when Israel keeps the mitzvot of God they will merit abundant blessing in grain, new wine and fresh oil. From grain one produces bread and other grain foods, from new wine – wine, and from fresh oil – oil (Devarim 7:13; 11:14). Similarly, the main part of the mitzva of terumot and ma'asrot is from grain, new wine and fresh oil (above 8:1). It follows that the decree not to eat the bread, wine and oil of non-Jews is a decree of principle, according to which the important foods of Israel must be of their own production. The second decree, on the cooked food of non-Jews, is directed straightforwardly against the personal closeness that may arise from eating the cooked dishes of non-Jews, even if they were prepared from foods belonging to Jews. Generally, by virtue of the decree on oil, the cooked food of non-Jews was also forbidden, since people were accustomed to flavour important dishes with oil. And when it became necessary to annul the decree on oil, the prohibition of the cooked food of non-Jews stood as a fence against excessive closeness that would lead to assimilation.

In summary, the decree of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on bread, oil and wine underwent changes. Oil, whose prohibition did not spread among the majority of Israel, was permitted entirely, and in its place the prohibition of the cooked dishes of non-Jews remained. With bread, they were lenient in a pressing situation with the "pat palter" of a non-Jew (below 28:2). And with wine, which can bring hearts closer together, they were more stringent, and forbade even the wine of a Jew that a non-Jew touched (below 29:1). And they further decreed not to drink alcoholic beverages in the home or shop of a non-Jew (below 29:11). Thus, in the end, the prohibitions remained attached to their main purpose, to prevent closeness that may lead to assimilation; and where there was no necessity to be stringent, as with oil – they were lenient, and likewise they were lenient in a pressing situation with "pat palter." And where it is fitting to be stringent, as with wine and alcoholic beverages, they added fences.5

notes_en.en:
At first, a line of reasoning was raised in the Talmud, Avoda Zara 37b, that the prohibition of the cooked food of non-Jews is from the Torah, and the conclusion of the Gemara is that the prohibition is rabbinic. In any case, we learn from this discussion that the prohibition of the cooked food of non-Jews has great force and a root in the Torah (as cited above in note 1).
According to the Ramban, Ra'ah and Ran, the decree on bread, oil and wine preceded the decree on the cooked food of non-Jews, for at first they decreed on the principal important foods that are eaten regularly and are essential for sustaining life. And in order to strengthen the enactment, they went further and decreed on the cooked food of non-Jews. And according to Rabbeinu Tam (Tosafot 37b, s.v. "ve-ha-shelakot"), the Rid and the Teruma, at first they decreed on the cooked dishes, in which there is more concern of closeness because their flavouring is more noticeable. And the students of Shammai and Hillel went further and decreed on bread, oil and wine, in order to raise the barriers against assimilation.

sections.title_en: Who Is Included in the Decree
sections.body_en:
All non-Jews are included in the prohibition of the bread and cooked food of non-Jews, and although the decree was intended to prevent marital ties, it also applies to non-Jews with whom there is no concern that they will marry Jews, such as the elderly, eunuchs or priests who vowed not to marry, for the Sages did not make distinctions in their decree (Responsa Rashba 1:248; Rema 112:1). This is because the concern is not that as a result of a Jew eating one food of a non-Jew he will immediately leap to marry the cook or the cook's daughter; rather, the concern is that the closeness of minds and the blurring of the boundaries between Jews and non-Jews will lead, in a gradual process, to assimilation. Therefore, they enacted that Jews should not eat the wine, bread and cooked dishes of non-Jews, and through this they will be educated to recognise their uniqueness, and will refrain from forming a personal connection with non-Jews that is too close, and will not come to assimilation. That is why they said (Avoda Zara 36b) that they decreed on their bread and their oil because of their wine, and on their wine because of their daughters, and on their daughters because of "something else," that is, idolatry, which expresses attaching oneself to a foreign culture. That is, if the concern had been only that people would come to the prohibition of marrying non-Jews, or only to the prohibition of idolatry while remaining in a Jewish identity, they would not have decreed on the foods of non-Jews. But since it is likely that through marital ties people will be drawn after a foreign culture and assimilate among the non-Jews, it was necessary to establish a system of fences intended to prevent assimilation. And since the decree is because of the concern of assimilation and not because of the prohibition of marriage, there is no prohibition for a Jew to eat the cooked dish of a Jew whom he is forbidden to marry, such as a mamzer or a married woman, since there is no concern of assimilation in this.6

Some say that the prohibition of the bread and cooked food of non-Jews also applies to Jewish apostates, that is, those who change their religion and do not keep the mitzvot of the Torah, because there is a concern that their bread and cooked food are not kosher, and one of the reasons for the prohibition of the cooked food of non-Jews is to set up a fence against eating non-kosher foods. However, in practice, since the essence of the decree was intended to prevent assimilation, these prohibitions do not apply to a Jew who does not keep Torah and mitzvot. However, from the standpoint of kashrut observance, one must indeed check thoroughly that the baked goods and cooked dishes he prepared are kosher (see below 38:9).7

notes_en.en:
In the Gemara, Avoda Zara 35b, it is explained that the prohibition of the bread of non-Jews is "because of ḥatnut (intermarriage)." And there, 36b, in explaining the decree on bread, oil and wine: "Rav Aḥa bar Ada said in the name of Rabbi Yitzḥak: They decreed… on their bread and their oil because of their wine, and on their wine because of their daughters, and on their daughters because of 'something else'" (that is, idolatry, and so it is explained in Shabbat 17b). And if the intention had been only to prevent idolatry, seemingly it should have been said that they decreed on bread, oil, wine and yiḥud (seclusion) because of idolatry; and from the fact that the Sages established a gradation in the decrees, decreeing on bread and oil because of wine, and on wine because of seclusion with their daughters, and on seclusion because of idolatry, it is evident that the intention is not to prevent a forbidden sexual relationship or idolatry in the narrow sense, but rather to prevent assimilation that will cause Jews to leave their people and their faith. Similarly wrote the Rambam (Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 17:9; Commentary on the Mishna, Avoda Zara 2:6), the Ramban (Avoda Zara 35b), the Ḥatam Sofer (Avoda Zara 55a) and the Alei Tamar (Yerushalmi Shabbat 1:4). Therefore there is no prohibition on the cooked food and bread of a mamzer, even though he is forbidden in marriage; and on the other hand, the bread and cooked food of non-Jews who are not idol worshippers are forbidden, as was ruled regarding Muslims (Rosh; Pri Toar 112:3; Pri Megadim 112, Siftei Da'at 2; Avnei Nezer YD 92; Rav Pe'alim YD 3:10; and unlike Torat Emet 112:1).
The prohibition of the bread and cooked food of non-Jews applies even when there is a concern of enmity between the Jew and the non-Jew (Taz YD 152:1, Knesset Ha-gedola, Pri Ḥadash 112:11, Ḥayim Be-yad by Rav Ḥayim Palagi. And the Mahariksh and Shulḥan Gavoha 112:9 were lenient regarding bread when there is a concern of enmity on the part of the ruler).

According to all the Rishonim, and so wrote Rashi on the Mishna 35b, the reason for the prohibition of the bread and cooked food of non-Jews is because of ḥatnut. However, Rashi (Avoda Zara 38a) and the Or Zarua added another reason for the prohibition, in order to distance people from eating forbidden foods that are commonly found among non-Jews. Accordingly, some sought to forbid the bread and cooked food of Jewish apostates, lest they feed them forbidden food. And they based their prohibition on what they learned from the Ran, that there is a rabbinic prohibition to marry a Jewish apostate, lest he turn one away from the ways of God, and so wrote the Yehuda Ya'aleh YD 31; Rav Shlomo Kluger, Tuv Ta'am Va-da'at, Mahadura Telita'a (third edition) 2:16; and see Yabi'a Omer 5, YD 10. However, the opinion of nearly all the poskim is that there is no prohibition of marriage with apostates, and so wrote the Ḥatam Sofer 2:120; 6:83; Erekh Ha-shulḥan 112:2; Maharshag 2:49. And so wrote the Tiferet Le-Moshe 113:9 and the Pitḥei Teshuva 112:1, that the main halakha is that the prohibition of the bread and cooked food of non-Jews is because of ḥatnut, and therefore there is no prohibition with the bread and cooked food of a Jewish apostate. And so wrote the Tzitz Eliezer 9:41.
It is worth noting that the words of those who forbid marriage with an apostate were said by the great Ashkenazic sages about a hundred and fifty years ago, in a period in which the chance that one who had left Judaism would return to its fold and not be absorbed among the nations was low, so that the reasoning that marriage with an apostate is similar to marriage with a non-Jew was understandable. However, today in the Land [of Israel], the chance of secular Jews drawing closer to tradition is much higher, and consequently the concern of assimilation as a result of marriage with a secular person is reduced.
